Key Findings

74.4% zero-visit rate — severe zero-inflation; 1,320 duplicates removed from raw data.

Reduced activity days strongest predictor (Spearman r = 0.403, p < 0.001).

Illness count drives ~10× rise in mean visits (r = 0.185, Kruskal-Wallis p = 5.7e-39).

Females visit more in every age group — gap peaks 30–44 (Mann-Whitney p < 0.0001).

Free government insurance removes cost barriers → highest observed visit rates.

Limiting chronic creates 2.2× visit multiplier; 11.7% of sample, outsized demand.

Self-rated health predicts visits monotonically (r = 0.149) — cheap screening signal.

Both classifiers AUC ≈ 0.71 on held-out test; ZINB / hurdle model recommended.

Exploratory Data Analysis — Figures 1–10
Fig 1 EDA §5.1

The Zero-Inflation Reality of Healthcare Utilisation

📖

After removing 1,320 duplicate records the clean dataset of 3,870 individuals shows roughly 3 in 4 people made zero doctor visits in the two-week window. The distribution is extremely right-skewed, with a tail reaching 9 visits. This zero-inflation is the central modelling challenge — standard OLS is inappropriate. Two-part hurdle or Negative Binomial models are required.

Fig 2 EDA §5.2

Gender & Age Dynamics in Healthcare Utilisation

📖

Females consistently visit more than males across every age band — linked to reproductive health, preventive care uptake, and greater help-seeking. The gap widens in the 30–44 band before converging at 60+ where chronic conditions equalise demand regardless of gender.

Fig 3 EDA §5.3

Illness Burden Drives Doctor Visits

📖

Illness count is the most direct lever on utilisation. As illnesses jump from 0 to 5, mean visits escalate nearly tenfold. The heatmap reveals a compounding nuance: poor self-rated health amplifies acute illness effects. Patients combining multiple illnesses with poor self-perception are the highest-burden group.

Fig 4 EDA §5.4

Socioeconomic Factors & Insurance Coverage

📖

Income tells a counterintuitive story: the lowest-income quartile visits most frequently — because this group disproportionately holds free government insurance, removing the cost barrier. The freepoor group visits ~50% more than the uninsured. It is the uninsured middle that falls through the cracks.

Fig 5 EDA §5.5

Chronic Illness Compounds Healthcare Demand

📖

Chronic illness is a care-demand multiplier. While most people average under 0.3 visits per fortnight, those with a limiting chronic condition average 2.2× as many. The boxplot shows visits among limiting-chronic patients are also wider and more right-skewed — a small group (11.7%) generating disproportionate demand.

Fig 6 EDA §5.6

Reduced Activity Days — The Sharpest Clinical Trigger

📖

Reduced activity days captures severity rather than just illness presence. When illness curtails daily life for 15+ days, mean visits jump nearly 3× baseline. At Spearman r = 0.403 this is the single strongest correlate of visit counts. 73% of respondents had zero reduced days — most people do not seek care for minor ailments.

Fig 7 EDA §5.7

Full Feature Correlation Matrix

📖

Reduced Days (r = 0.40) and Illness Count (r = 0.185) are the strongest positive correlates, followed by Health Score (r = 0.149), Age (r = 0.124), and FreeRepat insurance (r = 0.123). Income is slightly negative (r = −0.08). Insurance and demographic variables mostly show weak direct correlations — effects mediated through illness and health-status variables.

Fig 8 EDA §5.8

Self-Rated Health: Where Perception Meets Behaviour

📖

The self-rated health score has a broadly monotonic relationship with visits — people who perceive themselves as unwell seek care more. This variable captures behavioural intent: someone who feels unhealthy is more likely to translate that into a consultation regardless of clinical diagnosis. Cheap, scalable, and collectible in brief questionnaires.

Fig 9 EDA §5.9

Profiling High-Utilisation Patients (≥3 Visits)

📖

The high-utilisation profile (3+ visits) is clear: older females with limiting chronic conditions and free government insurance. Chronic patients cluster in the upper-right of the scatter — high illness counts AND high visit rates. Only 2.4% qualify as high utilisers yet they account for a disproportionate share of system demand.

Fig 10 EDA §5.11

Feature Distributions: Visitors vs. Non-Visitors (Violin Plots)

📖

Violin plots make the visitor/non-visitor separation immediate. Illness Count shows dramatic separation — visitors centre at 2–3 illnesses. Reduced Days is the most striking: visitors have a long right tail; non-visitors are nearly all zero. Health Score is markedly worse for visitors. Free-government-scheme holders have the highest visit rate; uninsured 'None' the lowest.

Predictive Modelling — Figures 12–14
Fig 12 Model §8a

Logistic & Poisson Regression — Interpretable Coefficients

📖

Stage 1 (Will they visit?): Illness Count, Reduced Days, and Health Score are the top three decision drivers. Female gender and Limiting Chronic also raise probability materially. Stage 2 (How many visits?): Reduced Days dominates repeat frequency among visitors. Together these form a hurdle model — the industry standard for zero-inflated count data. Logistic 5-fold CV AUC = 0.61.

Fig 13 Model §8b

Random Forest Feature Importance

📖

The Random Forest (stratified 5-fold CV AUC = 0.707 ± 0.004) confirms the logistic ranking. Reduced Days and Illness Count dominate both models. The RF additionally elevates Health Score and Age, reflecting non-linear interaction effects. Both models agree income and insurance dummies are weaker direct predictors — effects mediated through illness and severity.

Fig 14 Model §8c

ROC Curves & Confusion Matrices

📖

On the held-out test set both classifiers reach AUC ≈ 0.71. Both correctly identify most non-visitors (high specificity) but struggle on recall for visitors (74% vs 26% class imbalance). For healthcare resource planning recall matters most — a threshold-tuned Random Forest or full ZINB model would be the right deployment choice.

Strategic Recommendations
01

Use Zero-Inflated Count Models

ZINB or hurdle models required — OLS violates count-data assumptions.

02

Prioritise Reduced Activity Days

Strongest predictor (r = 0.40). Build alerts when patients report multiple reduced-activity days.

03

Target Chronic-Condition Patients

Older females + limiting chronic + multiple illnesses — predictable from admin data. Proactive management cuts repeat demand.

04

Address the Uninsured Middle

Mid-income uninsured show lower visit rates despite potential need. Cost barrier removal is the lever.

05

Deploy Self-Rated Health Screening

Predicts utilisation independently (r = 0.149). Cheap to collect via routine intake questionnaires.

06

Audit Data Collection Quality

25.5% of raw records were exact duplicates — a governance issue. Clean pipelines are prerequisite to any production model.
